text: There are n gas stations arranged in a circle. At station i you get gas of i. Driving from station i to the next station costs cost of i. You start with an empty tank. Return the index of the station where you can start and drive the full loop clockwise. If there is no such station, return negative one.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — at each station I first add the gas there, then pay the cost to reach the next one. The tank can hit exactly zero, but it can never go below zero. And a full loop means I come back to where I started. Is that right?
Yes. And if an answer exists, it's unique.

Good, that helps. Then the only number that really matters at each station is the net change — I'll call it diff, which is the gas at that station minus the cost to leave it. The tank after any stretch of road is just the sum of the diffs on that stretch. So I can think of the whole thing as a circle of numbers, and I need a starting point where the running sum never goes negative. Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and ten to the fifth, and every gas and cost value is between zero and ten to the fourth.

Got it. Up to a hundred thousand stations, so I want linear time. Let me run through the example. Gas is one, two, three, four, five, and cost is three, four, five, one, two, so the diffs are minus two, minus two, minus two, three, three. Starting at station three, the tank never dips below zero and comes back exactly empty, so the answer is three. That matches. The second example: gas two, three, four, cost three, four, three. The diffs add up to minus one — the loop burns more gas than it gives, so no start works, and the answer is negative one.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to try every start and simulate — quadratic, up to ten to the tenth steps, too slow. Starting at the biggest diff is also wrong: gas zero, one, two with cost three, zero, zero has its biggest diff at station two, but the answer is one. This problem reminds me of a greedy with a running sum, like Kadane's algorithm: when the sum goes negative, throw it away and start fresh. Why is that safe? A skip lemma. If I start at s and the tank first goes negative at i, nothing from s through i can be the start. Any station in between was reached with a tank of at least zero; starting there gives zero, so I'd fail at i again. So I jump the start straight to i plus one.
Okay. But after one pass, how do you know the last start you picked really works?

That's the second fact: an answer exists exactly when the total of all the diffs is at least zero. If it's negative, the loop costs more than it gives, so nothing works. If it's at least zero, the last candidate start works. From start to the end of the array, the running sum never went negative — that's how start survived. The part before start is made of pieces that each failed, and each piece only dips below zero at its very end. So the lowest point of the whole loop is the very end, where the tank holds exactly the total, which is at least zero. So there are two separate jobs: the total answers whether there's an answer at all, and cur with start answers which station it is.

Here's the plan. Three integers, all zero: total, cur, and start. First, for each station, compute the diff and add it to both total and cur. Second, if cur drops below zero, nothing from start through i works, so start moves to i plus one and cur resets to zero. Total is never reset. Third, return negative one if total is negative, otherwise start. One thing worth flagging — both comparisons are strict, on purpose. Cur less than zero, because an empty tank is still fine. And total less than zero, because a total of exactly zero is a valid loop — I come back empty, like in example one. Two passes would read a bit easier, but one pass does both jobs with three integers. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One loop: diff is gas of i minus cost of i, it goes into both total and cur, and when cur is below zero, start becomes i plus one and cur goes back to zero. After the loop, return negative one if total is below zero, otherwise start. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — start equals i plus one can end up equal to n, which is out of range. That only happens when the last station fails, which means every piece went negative, so the total is negative and I return negative one instead. And in my tests, returning start with no total check gets every single negative-one case wrong.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Example one, expected three. The first three stations each have a diff of minus two, so each start fails at once — that's the skip lemma — and start lands on three. The key row is i equals three: total is still minus three, but cur is three. They disagree because they do different jobs. Cur never goes negative again, and total ends at exactly zero, so the strict comparison returns three. Corner cases: one station with gas zero and cost one returns negative one, so the out-of-range start never leaks out. One station with gas and cost both zero returns zero — that single input catches both less-than-or-equal bugs. And against brute force on every small input, zero mismatches.

Let me think about complexity here. There's one loop over the stations. The start jumps forward, but it never moves back, and I never restart the loop. So each station is visited once. The time complexity is linear. The space complexity is constant: just total, cur, and start. In the worst-case scenario, the start resets at almost every station, like in example one. That's still constant work per station. The skip lemma is what lets me never look back. Oh, one more thing — overflow. Total sums up to ten to the fifth diffs, each between minus ten to the fourth and ten to the fourth. So the absolute value of total is at most ten to the ninth, which is below the maximum int. A plain int is safe here. If the limits were bigger, I'd switch to long long.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You proved the skip lemma: if the tank fails at i, nothing from start through i can work, so one pass is enough. You split the two jobs: a non-negative total says an answer exists, and you explained why the last start is that answer. And you defended both strict comparisons with one tiny input — gas zero, cost zero — where the tank ends empty. Good work.
